doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Race, education and the future of jazz
title: Proposal: artist residencies with veteran musicians
summary: She urges campuses to host veteran musicians for residencies, and says teachers may feel threatened.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I think that you’re going in the right direction, you’re certainly going in the right direction here with people like Milt Fillius and what you’re doing, Monk. I think certainly. You can encourage. There are a lot of people at Bob’s age group who are more than happy to come on to your campus and spend a month doing an Artist in Residency. They are sitting around not necessarily wanting to be running for gigs all the time, but they would be happy to pass on their legacy and to come in and be articulate and talking — not to be threatening the teachers, they’re not looking to take over a full time job with tenure at a university. But they would be delighted I think to come in and talk about what it really is like to be a street musician, not just an academic, not somebody who’s graduated with a bachelor’s degree and taken a job right away. All right?

Now. I think that it is possible — you’re looking for an answer? I’m going to give you one, all right? I am not a wishy-washy person. I’m going to tell you that you look around the country. There are people who are articulate musicians, who would be happy to give you two weeks of their time, you accommodate them, you treat them as well as you have been treating us, and you say talk to our students. Tell them about the relevance of this music. And you bring in somebody else. And you bring in somebody else. And you bring in somebody else. You can get funding for doing these kinds of things. And I have to say that more often than not — do you know who’s going to be more upset than anybody? I don’t know whether it’s this way here, but I’ll tell you on most of the academic campuses we go — are the teachers. Because what you’re doing is almost teaching sedition. You are teaching these students, you’re telling these students something that maybe is opening up a Pandora’s box because baby, the teacher is suddenly out on a limb. He doesn’t know maybe about that period perhaps that you’re going to talk about. But people shouldn’t be threatened. The whole idea of being in teaching is not to be threatened, but to give of your own ability and learn, keep your own ears open. And to have these kids being given every opportunity. Now I know for instance that in Arizona that there are two very good academic programs in music. My husband has not been asked to do anything, even though he’d be happy to go up there and give his time, just to sort of make sure that the legacy is passed on. Why don’t they want him? What if he goes in there and tells the real story of what jazz is about? Not some far-reaching fantasy. What if he just goes in there and just says look I’m Bob Wilber and this is what I’ve done all my life, and there are many other people like him who would be delighted to do this. Wouldn’t that be a good idea? Wouldn’t that be one way of salvaging what is left, and hoping that you’re going to give jazz music the credibility that it should have, the place in American society is to start with young people. And when young people hear Bob talk, and hear these legends talk, they have a whole excitement about what they’re learning. I don’t know what to say. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
